cards.question_text: What is the key difference between a stateless (packet-filtering) firewall and a stateful firewall?
choices: A stateless firewall filters each packet in isolation using only ACL rules (IP, port, protocol), while a stateful firewall tracks the state of connections (SYN, ESTABLISHED, FIN) and can allow return traffic for an established session
A stateless firewall is faster because it inspects the full packet payload, while a stateful firewall only looks at headers
A stateful firewall can only block traffic but never allow it, while a stateless firewall can do both
A stateless firewall operates at Layer 7 only, while a stateful firewall operates at Layer 3 only
cards.answer: A stateless firewall filters each packet in isolation using only ACL rules (IP, port, protocol), while a stateful firewall tracks the state of connections (SYN, ESTABLISHED, FIN) and can allow return traffic for an established session
cards.explanation_correct: Stateless firewalls evaluate each packet independently against static rules — they don't know if a packet is part of an existing connection. Stateful firewalls maintain a state table that tracks active connections, so when an internal host initiates a connection, the firewall automatically allows the return traffic. This makes stateful firewalls more secure and easier to configure, since you don't need explicit rules for return traffic.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B reverses the inspection depth — stateless is simpler, not deeper. Option C is nonsensical — both can allow and block. Option D is backwards — stateless typically operates at Layers 3-4, stateful can also operate at those layers plus track session state.

cards.question_text: What is a Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW), and what capability distinguishes it from a traditional stateful firewall?
choices: An NGFW combines traditional stateful filtering with deep packet inspection, application awareness (identifying specific apps like Facebook or BitTorrent regardless of port), integrated IPS/IDS, and threat intelligence feeds
An NGFW is a firewall that uses AI to automatically block all unknown traffic without any administrator configuration
An NGFW is a cloud-only firewall that cannot be deployed on-premises
An NGFW is identical to a stateful firewall but runs on faster hardware
cards.answer: An NGFW combines traditional stateful filtering with deep packet inspection, application awareness (identifying specific apps like Facebook or BitTorrent regardless of port), integrated IPS/IDS, and threat intelligence feeds
cards.explanation_correct: NGFWs go beyond port/protocol filtering. They inspect packet payloads to identify the actual application (e.g., detecting SSH traffic on port 443), integrate intrusion prevention, and can use real-time threat intelligence to block known-malicious IPs/domains. This application-layer awareness is the key differentiator — a traditional firewall sees 'TCP port 443' while an NGFW sees 'WhatsApp over TCP 443' and can apply app-specific policies.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is wrong — NGFWs still require configuration and policy rules. Option C is wrong — NGFWs are deployed both on-premises and in the cloud. Option D misses the point — the difference is capability, not hardware speed.

cards.question_text: A company discovers that employees are using personal cloud storage services (like Dropbox) over HTTPS to exfiltrate sensitive data. Their current stateful firewall allows outbound TCP 443. What is the most effective firewall upgrade to address this?
choices: Deploy an NGFW with application awareness to identify and block specific cloud storage applications (Dropbox, Google Drive) even though they use port 443, while still allowing legitimate HTTPS web traffic
Block all outbound TCP 443 traffic entirely — this stops all encrypted exfiltration
Replace the stateful firewall with a stateless packet filter and block Dropbox's known IP addresses
Add a rule to block all traffic to any IP address outside Singapore
cards.answer: Deploy an NGFW with application awareness to identify and block specific cloud storage applications (Dropbox, Google Drive) even though they use port 443, while still allowing legitimate HTTPS web traffic
cards.explanation_correct: The problem is that Dropbox and similar services use standard HTTPS (port 443), so port-based filtering can't distinguish them from legitimate web traffic. An NGFW with application awareness performs deep packet inspection to identify the specific application protocol within the TLS session (via SNI, certificate analysis, or TLS fingerprinting), allowing granular policies: block Dropbox but allow access to legitimate HTTPS sites. Blocking all 443 would break most web browsing.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B breaks nearly all web browsing — most sites use HTTPS. Option C is ineffective — cloud services use many dynamic IPs and CDNs, and stateless filtering is a downgrade. Option D is overly broad and would block legitimate international business sites.

cards.question_text: A web application is receiving SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks from the internet. The company already has a stateful firewall at the network perimeter. What additional security control should they deploy specifically to protect the web application layer?
choices: A Web Application Firewall (WAF) that inspects HTTP/HTTPS traffic at Layer 7, filtering malicious requests based on OWASP rulesets (SQLi, XSS, CSRF patterns) before they reach the web server
A second stateful firewall placed behind the web server for defense in depth
An IDS configured in passive mode that logs SQL injection attempts for later review
A VPN concentrator that requires all web visitors to authenticate before accessing the site
cards.answer: A Web Application Firewall (WAF) that inspects HTTP/HTTPS traffic at Layer 7, filtering malicious requests based on OWASP rulesets (SQLi, XSS, CSRF patterns) before they reach the web server
cards.explanation_correct: A WAF operates at Layer 7 (application layer), inspecting the actual HTTP request content — query strings, headers, body payloads — to detect and block SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, and other web-specific attacks. A stateful firewall operates at Layers 3-4 and cannot inspect HTTP payloads. The WAF sits in front of the web server (reverse proxy mode) and blocks malicious requests before they reach the application. WAFs use signature-based, behavioral, and heuristic detection against OWASP Top 10 threats.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B adds another Layer 3-4 firewall — it still can't inspect HTTP payloads. Option C (IDS in passive mode) only logs, doesn't block — an IPS would block, but a WAF is purpose-built for web attacks. Option D would break public access to the website.

cards.question_text: A network engineer is configuring firewall rules and needs to follow the principle of 'default deny.' What does this mean, and how should the final rule be configured?
choices: Default deny means the last rule in the ACL blocks all traffic that hasn't been explicitly allowed by earlier rules — every permitted connection must have an explicit allow rule, and anything unmatched is dropped
Default deny means the firewall denies traffic by default but allows all traffic if no rules are configured
Default deny means only deny rules are used, and no allow rules are ever needed
Default deny means the firewall blocks traffic from denylisted IPs but allows everything else by default
cards.answer: Default deny means the last rule in the ACL blocks all traffic that hasn't been explicitly allowed by earlier rules — every permitted connection must have an explicit allow rule, and anything unmatched is dropped
cards.explanation_correct: Default deny (also called 'deny all, allow by exception') is the most secure firewall posture. The ACL contains explicit allow rules for each permitted service/flow, and the final catch-all rule denies everything else. This means any new service or protocol automatically gets blocked unless an administrator deliberately adds a rule for it. The opposite — default allow — is dangerous because new services are automatically permitted.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is the opposite of default deny. Option C is wrong — allow rules are absolutely needed; default deny just means everything else is denied. Option D describes a denylist approach, which is default allow (the less secure posture).

cards.question_text: What is the fundamental difference between an Intrusion Detection System (IDS) and an Intrusion Prevention System (IPS)?
choices: An IDS detects and alerts on suspicious activity but does not block it (passive/out-of-band), while an IPS detects AND actively blocks or drops malicious traffic (active/in-line)
An IDS is hardware-based and an IPS is software-based
An IDS monitors network traffic and an IPS monitors host activity only
An IDS uses signatures and an IPS uses behavioral analysis only — they use different detection methods
cards.answer: An IDS detects and alerts on suspicious activity but does not block it (passive/out-of-band), while an IPS detects AND actively blocks or drops malicious traffic (active/in-line)
cards.explanation_correct: The key distinction is response: an IDS is a detective control — it sends alerts when it detects suspicious patterns but the traffic still reaches its destination. An IPS is a preventive control — it sits in-line (inline) with traffic flow and can drop malicious packets before they reach the target. IDS is typically deployed out-of-band using a SPAN/mirror port. IPS must be in-line to block. Both can use signature-based and anomaly-based detection.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is wrong — both can be hardware or software. Option C is wrong — both can monitor network or host (NIDS/NIPS vs HIDS/HIPS). Option D is wrong — both IDS and IPS can use signatures AND behavioral analysis; the difference is response, not detection method.

cards.question_text: What is the difference between signature-based detection and anomaly-based (heuristic) detection in an IDS/IPS?
choices: Signature-based compares traffic against a database of known attack patterns (like antivirus definitions); anomaly-based establishes a baseline of normal behavior and flags deviations from that baseline
Signature-based uses AI to predict future attacks; anomaly-based only looks at past traffic logs
Signature-based detects zero-day attacks; anomaly-based only detects known attacks
Signature-based is always more accurate than anomaly-based in all scenarios
cards.answer: Signature-based compares traffic against a database of known attack patterns (like antivirus definitions); anomaly-based establishes a baseline of normal behavior and flags deviations from that baseline
cards.explanation_correct: Signature-based detection is like pattern matching — it has a database of known attack signatures (e.g., a specific SQL injection string, a known malware C2 beacon) and alerts when traffic matches. It's fast and accurate for known threats but misses zero-day attacks. Anomaly-based detection learns what 'normal' looks like (traffic volume, port usage, login times) and alerts on significant deviations. It can catch novel attacks but produces more false positives because legitimate unusual behavior also triggers alerts.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B reverses the concepts. Option C is the opposite — signature-based misses zero-days, anomaly-based can potentially catch them. Option D is wrong — anomaly-based can be more accurate for novel attacks; each method has different strengths.

cards.question_text: A company deploys a network-based IDS (NIDS) using a SPAN/mirror port on their core switch. They notice the IDS is missing some attack traffic. Investigation shows the switch port is oversubscribed — traffic exceeds the SPAN port's capacity during peak hours. What is the consequence and how should it be addressed?
choices: The switch drops mirrored packets during peak traffic, causing the IDS to miss attacks — replace the SPAN-based IDS with an in-line IPS (network tap or in-line deployment) that sees 100% of traffic without oversubscription
The IDS will detect more attacks because the dropped packets reduce noise — no action needed
Move the IDS to a different VLAN to reduce traffic load
Increase the IDS alert sensitivity threshold to compensate for dropped packets
cards.answer: The switch drops mirrored packets during peak traffic, causing the IDS to miss attacks — replace the SPAN-based IDS with an in-line IPS (network tap or in-line deployment) that sees 100% of traffic without oversubscription
cards.explanation_correct: SPAN/mirror ports have limited bandwidth — if the monitored traffic exceeds the mirror port's capacity, the switch silently drops excess mirrored packets. The IDS never sees them, creating blind spots during exactly the high-traffic periods when attacks are most likely to be hidden. An in-line IPS or a network TAP (Test Access Point) avoids this because it processes traffic in-line at full line rate — no mirroring, no oversubscription. A hardware TAP provides a permanent, passive copy of traffic at full speed.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is dangerous — dropped packets mean missed attacks, not less noise. Option C doesn't solve the core issue — the IDS would still miss traffic on the monitored VLAN. Option D is nonsensical — increasing sensitivity doesn't compensate for packets the IDS never received.

cards.question_text: A security team deploys a HIDS (Host-based IDS) on all Windows servers. What type of threats can the HIDS detect that a NIDS (Network-based IDS) positioned at the perimeter would likely miss?
choices: Unauthorized file changes on the server's filesystem, suspicious local process execution, and lateral movement via encrypted internal traffic — all of which occur on the host itself and may never traverse the network perimeter
Port scans originating from the internet against the company's public-facing servers
DDoS volumetric attacks flooding the company's internet connection
Network-level packet crafting attacks against the perimeter firewall
cards.answer: Unauthorized file changes on the server's filesystem, suspicious local process execution, and lateral movement via encrypted internal traffic — all of which occur on the host itself and may never traverse the network perimeter
cards.explanation_correct: A HIDS monitors the host directly — filesystem integrity, running processes, system logs, registry changes, and local network connections. It detects threats that never cross the network perimeter: an insider modifying files locally, malware that's already on the host, or lateral movement over encrypted channels (RDP, SSH) that a NIDS can't inspect. A NIDS sees network traffic at the perimeter but is blind to host-internal activity and encrypted east-west traffic. Defense in depth means using both.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Options B, C, and D are all network-level threats that a NIDS at the perimeter is well-positioned to detect — they involve traffic crossing the network boundary. The HIDS's unique value is visibility into what's happening ON the host itself.

cards.question_text: What is a VLAN, and how does it contribute to network security?
choices: A VLAN (Virtual LAN) is a logical grouping of devices on a switch that creates separate broadcast domains at Layer 2 — devices in different VLANs cannot communicate without a router or Layer 3 firewall, isolating traffic between segments
A VLAN is a physical separation of network cables into different rooms
A VLAN encrypts all traffic between devices on the same switch
A VLAN is a VPN tunnel that connects remote offices securely
cards.answer: A VLAN (Virtual LAN) is a logical grouping of devices on a switch that creates separate broadcast domains at Layer 2 — devices in different VLANs cannot communicate without a router or Layer 3 firewall, isolating traffic between segments
cards.explanation_correct: VLANs segment a physical switch into multiple logical networks. Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain — broadcast traffic (ARP, DHCP) stays within the VLAN. Inter-VLAN traffic must pass through a router or Layer 3 switch/firewall where ACLs can control access. This limits the blast radius: if a device in the guest VLAN is compromised, the attacker cannot directly reach servers in the production VLAN without traversing a controlled routing boundary.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B describes physical isolation, not VLANs (which are logical). Option C is wrong — VLANs don't encrypt; encryption is handled by protocols like TLS/IPsec. Option D confuses VLANs with VPNs — they are completely different technologies.

cards.question_text: A hospital network has medical devices (infusion pumps, MRI machines), guest Wi-Fi, and an electronic health records (EHR) system all on the same flat network. A security consultant recommends segmenting these into separate VLANs with a firewall controlling inter-VLAN traffic. What is the primary security benefit?
choices: If a guest's compromised laptop attempts to spread malware, the firewall between VLANs blocks lateral movement to medical devices and the EHR system — each segment is isolated and traffic between them is explicitly controlled
Segmentation will make the network faster by reducing the number of IP addresses needed
Segmentation eliminates the need for any other security controls like antivirus or patching
Segmentation ensures all devices get the same level of access for simplicity
cards.answer: If a guest's compromised laptop attempts to spread malware, the firewall between VLANs blocks lateral movement to medical devices and the EHR system — each segment is isolated and traffic between them is explicitly controlled
cards.explanation_correct: On a flat network, any compromised device can reach any other device — a guest laptop can scan and exploit medical devices or the EHR system. VLAN segmentation with firewall enforcement creates security zones: guest traffic stays in the guest VLAN, medical devices in a medical IoT VLAN (with strict allow rules only for required protocols), and the EHR in a protected VLAN. The firewall only permits explicitly allowed inter-VLAN flows (e.g., EHR server → database port), blocking everything else. This is critical in healthcare where medical device compromise can be life-threatening.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is a side effect, not the security benefit. Option C is wrong — segmentation is defense in depth, not a replacement for other controls. Option D is the opposite of segmentation's purpose — different segments get different access levels.

cards.question_text: An organization's internal network uses a flat topology — all servers and workloads are on the same subnet. After a phishing attack compromises one workstation, the attacker pivots to multiple internal servers within minutes. What network design change would most effectively limit this lateral movement?
choices: Implement microsegmentation — place each critical workload (or small group) in its own segment with granular firewall rules controlling exactly which other workloads can communicate with it, limiting an attacker's east-west movement
Install antivirus on all workstations and run a full scan
Move all servers to a single new VLAN but leave workstations on the old network
Change all server passwords and require longer user passwords
cards.answer: Implement microsegmentation — place each critical workload (or small group) in its own segment with granular firewall rules controlling exactly which other workloads can communicate with it, limiting an attacker's east-west movement
cards.explanation_correct: In a flat network, once an attacker compromises one host, they can scan and attack any other host on the same subnet — there's no internal boundary. Microsegmentation creates fine-grained zones (down to individual workloads) with explicit allow rules: a web server can only talk to the app server on specific ports, the app server can only talk to the database on port 3306. This means compromising the web server doesn't give access to the file server or other unrelated systems. East-west traffic (server-to-server) is the primary vector for lateral movement, and microsegmentation directly addresses it.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B (antivirus) is important but doesn't address the network architecture problem — it detects malware, not lateral movement. Option C is a coarse improvement but doesn't stop an attacker who reaches the server VLAN. Option D is a credential control, not a network control — it doesn't prevent lateral movement through compromised accounts.

cards.question_text: What is east-west traffic in a data center context, and why is it a security concern that differs from north-south traffic?
choices: East-west traffic is server-to-server communication within the data center (internal), while north-south is traffic entering/leaving the data center (external). East-west is a concern because perimeter firewalls don't see it — lateral movement happens internally between compromised and target systems
East-west traffic is traffic between data centers in different geographic regions; north-south is traffic within a single data center
East-west traffic refers to traffic during business hours; north-south refers to after-hours traffic
East-west traffic is encrypted traffic; north-south is unencrypted traffic
cards.answer: East-west traffic is server-to-server communication within the data center (internal), while north-south is traffic entering/leaving the data center (external). East-west is a concern because perimeter firewalls don't see it — lateral movement happens internally between compromised and target systems
cards.explanation_correct: In modern data centers, the vast majority of traffic is east-west — server-to-server communication (web→app→database, microservice-to-microservice). Traditional perimeter security focuses on north-south (internet→DMZ→internal), but once an attacker breaches the perimeter, they move east-west between servers. Perimeter firewalls don't inspect this internal traffic. This is why microsegmentation and internal firewalls/IPS are critical — they bring firewall enforcement to the east-west plane where most modern attack movement occurs.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B reverses the definitions. Option C is a made-up distinction based on time of day. Option D is wrong — both east-west and north-south traffic can be encrypted or unencrypted; the terms describe traffic direction, not encryption.

cards.question_text: What is a DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) in network architecture, and what is its purpose?
choices: A DMZ is a isolated network segment (screened subnet) placed between the internet and the internal network, hosting public-facing services (web, email, DNS) so that if they're compromised, the attacker still faces a firewall before reaching internal systems
A DMZ is a military-grade encryption standard used for government networks
A DMZ is a backup network that activates only when the primary network fails
A DMZ is a zone where all traffic is allowed without filtering to maximize performance
cards.answer: A DMZ is a isolated network segment (screened subnet) placed between the internet and the internal network, hosting public-facing services (web, email, DNS) so that if they're compromised, the attacker still faces a firewall before reaching internal systems
cards.explanation_correct: A DMZ (also called a screened subnet or perimeter network) is a buffer zone between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network. Public-facing servers (web, mail, DNS) are placed in the DMZ because they must be accessible from the internet and are therefore higher-risk. If an attacker compromises a DMZ server, they are still separated from the internal network by an internal firewall. The DMZ is typically separated from both the internet and the internal network by firewalls (two-firewall architecture: external firewall → DMZ → internal firewall → LAN).
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B confuses the military term with network architecture. Option C describes a failover network, not a DMZ. Option D is the opposite of a DMZ's purpose — it's a controlled, filtered zone, not an open one.

cards.question_text: What is the 'defense in depth' principle as applied to network security architecture?
choices: Layering multiple independent security controls (firewall, IDS/IPS, endpoint protection, encryption, access control) so that if one fails, others still protect the system — no single point of failure
Deploying many firewalls in a row to maximize packet inspection depth
Hiring more security analysts to monitor the network in shifts
Making the network architecture documentation extremely detailed
cards.answer: Layering multiple independent security controls (firewall, IDS/IPS, endpoint protection, encryption, access control) so that if one fails, others still protect the system — no single point of failure
cards.explanation_correct: Defense in depth assumes no single control is perfect. If the perimeter firewall is misconfigured, the IDS may still detect the intrusion. If malware gets past the firewall, endpoint protection may catch it. If an attacker steals credentials, MFA may still block them. Each layer addresses different attack vectors and failure modes. The layers should be independent — a vulnerability in one shouldn't disable the others. Classic layers: physical security → perimeter firewall → DMZ → internal firewall → host hardening → application security → data encryption.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is a narrow interpretation — defense in depth is about diverse control types, not just more firewalls. Option C is about staffing, not architecture. Option D confuses documentation depth with security depth.

cards.question_text: A company has a public-facing web server and an internal database server. The web server needs to query the database. A junior administrator proposes placing both servers on the same internal subnet for simplicity. Why is this a security risk, and what is the better architecture?
choices: If the web server is compromised (it's internet-facing), placing it on the internal subnet gives the attacker direct access to the database and the entire internal network — the web server should be in a DMZ, and the database should be on the internal network behind a firewall that only allows the web server's IP on the specific database port
It's not a risk — placing them together reduces latency and simplifies management
Both servers should be placed in the DMZ so they're equally accessible
The database should be placed in the DMZ and the web server on the internal network
cards.answer: If the web server is compromised (it's internet-facing), placing it on the internal subnet gives the attacker direct access to the database and the entire internal network — the web server should be in a DMZ, and the database should be on the internal network behind a firewall that only allows the web server's IP on the specific database port
cards.explanation_correct: The web server is internet-facing and therefore at higher risk of compromise. If it's on the internal subnet, an attacker who exploits it has a foothold inside the trusted network with access to the database and all internal systems. The correct architecture: web server in the DMZ, database on the internal network. An internal firewall allows only the web server's IP address to connect to the database on the specific port (e.g., 3306/5432), and nothing else. This way, even if the web server is compromised, the attacker can only reach the database — not file servers, workstations, or other internal systems.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B prioritizes convenience over security — a common but dangerous mistake. Option C puts the database in the DMZ, exposing it to the internet — databases should never be internet-accessible. Option D reverses the correct placement — the web server needs to be in the DMZ (public-facing), not the database.

cards.question_text: An organization needs to provide SSH access for remote administrators to an internal jump server. The jump server then connects to internal production servers. What is this architecture called, and what security benefit does it provide?
choices: This is a bastion host (jump box) architecture — all administrative access flows through a single hardened, monitored choke point, so the bastion can enforce MFA, log all sessions, and restrict which internal servers each admin can reach — internal servers never need to be directly exposed to the internet
This is a VPN architecture — the jump server encrypts all traffic between the admin and the internal network
This is a load balancer architecture — the jump server distributes SSH connections across multiple servers
This is a honeypot architecture — the jump server is designed to attract attackers
cards.answer: This is a bastion host (jump box) architecture — all administrative access flows through a single hardened, monitored choke point, so the bastion can enforce MFA, log all sessions, and restrict which internal servers each admin can reach — internal servers never need to be directly exposed to the internet
cards.explanation_correct: A bastion host (jump box) is the only server exposed to the internet for administrative access. It's heavily hardened (minimal services, strong authentication, full logging). Admins SSH to the bastion, then from the bastion to internal servers. Benefits: (1) internal servers aren't exposed to the internet, (2) all admin activity is logged at a single point, (3) MFA and access policies are enforced at one choke point, (4) if an admin's credentials are stolen, the attacker still needs to get through the bastion. Modern equivalents include PAM (Privileged Access Management) solutions and Zero Trust access brokers.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B confuses a bastion host with a VPN — a VPN provides network-level access, while a bastion provides application-level relay with monitoring. Option C describes load balancing, not administrative access. Option D describes a honeypot (deception), not a jump server.

cards.question_text: What is the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy?
choices: A forward proxy sits between internal clients and the internet, intercepting outbound traffic (often for filtering, caching, or anonymity); a reverse proxy sits in front of web servers, intercepting inbound traffic from the internet (for load balancing, WAF, caching, or TLS termination)
A forward proxy speeds up traffic by forwarding packets faster; a reverse proxy slows down traffic for inspection
A forward proxy is used for email; a reverse proxy is used for web browsing
A forward proxy encrypts traffic; a reverse proxy decrypts traffic
cards.answer: A forward proxy sits between internal clients and the internet, intercepting outbound traffic (often for filtering, caching, or anonymity); a reverse proxy sits in front of web servers, intercepting inbound traffic from the internet (for load balancing, WAF, caching, or TLS termination)
cards.explanation_correct: A forward proxy (like Squid) is client-side: internal users' web traffic goes through the proxy, which can filter URLs, cache content, log activity, and hide the client's IP. A reverse proxy (like Nginx, HAProxy, Cloudflare) is server-side: it receives requests from the internet and forwards them to backend servers. Reverse proxies provide load balancing, TLS termination (offloading SSL from backend servers), WAF functionality, and DDoS protection. The key distinction: forward proxy protects the client, reverse proxy protects the server.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is about speed, not the architectural difference. Option C is wrong — both primarily handle web/HTTP traffic. Option D is wrong — both can encrypt or decrypt; the difference is traffic direction, not encryption.

cards.question_text: A company deploys a reverse proxy (Nginx) in front of three identical web servers. The reverse proxy handles TLS termination and distributes requests using round-robin. What are the key benefits of this architecture compared to exposing the web servers directly?
choices: TLS termination offloads encryption from the web servers (saving CPU), the backend servers' IP addresses are hidden from the internet (internal IPs not exposed), and load is distributed across three servers — improving performance, security, and availability
The reverse proxy automatically patches vulnerabilities on all three web servers
The reverse proxy ensures all three servers return identical content by merging their responses
The reverse proxy eliminates the need for any firewall because it filters all malicious traffic
cards.answer: TLS termination offloads encryption from the web servers (saving CPU), the backend servers' IP addresses are hidden from the internet (internal IPs not exposed), and load is distributed across three servers — improving performance, security, and availability
cards.explanation_correct: A reverse proxy provides multiple benefits: (1) TLS termination — the proxy handles SSL/TLS, so backend servers communicate over plain HTTP internally, saving CPU and simplifying certificate management. (2) IP hiding — the internet only sees the proxy's IP; backend servers have private IPs and aren't directly reachable, reducing attack surface. (3) Load balancing — requests are distributed across servers, so if one fails, the others continue serving. (4) The proxy can also add WAF rules, rate limiting, and caching. This is the standard architecture for production web deployments.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is wrong — proxies don't patch servers. Option C is wrong — the proxy distributes requests, it doesn't merge responses. Option D overstates the proxy's role — a firewall is still needed; the proxy handles HTTP-layer filtering but not network-layer security.

cards.question_text: A school wants to prevent students from accessing social media and gaming sites while on the campus Wi-Fi. They also want to log all web browsing activity for compliance. What type of proxy should they deploy, and how should it be configured?
choices: A forward proxy (like Squid) configured as a transparent proxy or via PAC file — all student web traffic routes through the proxy, which checks each URL against a blocklist/category filter, logs the request (student ID, URL, timestamp), and allows or denies accordingly
A reverse proxy placed in front of the school's web server to filter incoming traffic
A VPN concentrator that encrypts all student traffic and blocks social media at the VPN layer
A firewall rule that blocks all outbound traffic except port 443
cards.answer: A forward proxy (like Squid) configured as a transparent proxy or via PAC file — all student web traffic routes through the proxy, which checks each URL against a blocklist/category filter, logs the request (student ID, URL, timestamp), and allows or denies accordingly
cards.explanation_correct: A forward proxy is designed for exactly this use case. It intercepts outbound web traffic from clients (students) and applies URL filtering (blocking social media, gaming, adult content categories), logging (who accessed what and when), and caching (speeding up frequently accessed educational content). It can be deployed transparently (redirecting traffic at the network layer via WCCP or iptables) or via a PAC file (proxy auto-configuration). The proxy can authenticate users to tie browsing activity to specific students. This is a classic forward proxy / content filtering deployment.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is wrong — a reverse proxy handles inbound traffic to servers, not outbound student browsing. Option C is overkill and doesn't provide URL-level filtering. Option D only blocks by port, not by URL/category — social media sites use port 443 (HTTPS), so this would block nothing.
